activities.caption: call the magnitude — electrocution's share of the toll
activities.name: esOshaEstimate

config.prompt: Per OSHA's own studies, what share of construction worker deaths in an average year does electrocution account for?
config.why: Roughly one in thirty — and the great majority trace back to skipped procedure, not unknown physics.
config.context: A hot exhaust pipe hisses, a rotten beam creaks, a gas leak smells — a lethal conductor looks exactly like a dead one.

activities.anchor: Electricity threatens in three distinct ways
activities.caption: pair each killer with the response that defeats it
activities.name: esThreatMatch

config.prompt: Every safety rule maps onto one of the three killers — pair threat with answer:

pairs.right: conductors and breakers sized so nothing overheats

config.why: Each card pairs a hazard with the response that defeats it — and the physics card sits in the middle because Ohm's law is the arithmetic underneath every defence, from breaker ratings to voltage-drop limits.

activities.caption: series or parallel? file the behaviour
activities.name: esArrangementBuckets

config.prompt: Two arrangements, one instant recognition — file each behaviour:

items.label: old Christmas lights: one dead bulb darkens the string
every branch sees the full voltage
one dead branch does not disturb the others

config.why: Buildings are wired in parallel — every outlet full voltage, the kettle switching off without darkening the kitchen — but every branch added draws more total current, and total current is what heats the supply cables.

activities.anchor: Wet skin can drop to around 1,000
activities.caption: bet the current before the arithmetic
activities.name: esWetPredict

config.q: A 230 V socket meets damp hands — roughly how much current is driven through the chest?
config.why: I = V ÷ R gives 0.23 A — far past the 30–50 mA where the heart's rhythm can collapse. It is current you must keep out of your body; voltage together with body resistance decides how much gets in — hence bathrooms, rain-soaked sites and damp grips slow the trade down.

activities.caption: stack Dalziel's stages as the current climbs
activities.name: esDalzielOrder

config.prompt: From tingle to fibrillation — put the stages in order of current:
items: A few milliamps — a painful jolt, but you can still pull away
10–30 mA — muscles seize: the "cannot let go" range
Above about 30–50 mA across the chest — ventricular fibrillation
config.why: The "cannot let go" range is where the hand grips the very conductor it should release — and the whole scale is thousandths of an amp, not amps.

activities.caption: walk the procedure — what does each step defeat?
activities.name: esProcedureBranch

config.root: Hands are about to go into a panel. Walk the drilled procedure and say what each step defeats.

start.text: First move — why begin by cutting the supply rather than 'being careful'?

choices.label: A live conductor looks exactly like a dead one — no hiss, no glow, no smell
choices.feedback: The hazard gives no warning, so perception is replaced with procedure.

choices.label: An experienced hand can see danger coming
choices.feedback: Silent, invisible, instantaneous — electricity does not give second chances at belief.

choices.label: Careful work at 230 V is safe enough
choices.feedback: Household 230 V kills routinely — energised until proven dead is the professional's default.

lock.text: Supply cut. What do lock and tag defeat?

choices.label: Anyone re-energising while your hands are in the panel
choices.feedback: Lockout/tagout — it exists because "just a second" has killed.

choices.label: Static discharge from the cable
choices.feedback: Not the adversary here — the risk is another person restoring power.

choices.label: The arc-flash hazard
choices.feedback: That exposure has its own standard (NFPA 70E); lock and tag defeat people, not plasma.

test.text: Locked and tagged. What does the final 'prove' defeat?

choices.label: A lying meter — flat battery, blown fuse, wrong dial, wrong pair of conductors
choices.feedback: A dead reading bracketed by two live proofs is the only evidence the trade accepts.

choices.label: A re-energised panel
choices.feedback: That was lock and tag's job — proving is about the instrument, not the panel.

choices.label: Nothing — it is ceremony
choices.feedback: It is the step skipped in most of the accidents OSHA counts.

end.text: De-energise, lock, tag, test, prove — a zero energy state: every source of harmful energy secured, not merely switched off.

config.why: Even good procedure cannot drive risk to zero — never grab a person still in contact with a live conductor; cut the power or break contact with an insulating object first.

activities.anchor: Every conductor resists, so every run
activities.caption: fill the voltage-drop arithmetic
activities.name: esDropCloze

config.text: Every metre of cable loses voltage: drop = %%0%% × R, growing as the run gets longer and shrinking as the wire gets %%1%%. A motor starved of voltage draws %%2%% current to do the same work, heats itself further and can burn out — which is why codes cap the drop near 3–%%3%% per cent.
config.hint: Three sliders, one line of arithmetic, and a codebook consequence — the fix is always bigger copper.

activities.anchor: Every diagnosis in the trade is this loop
activities.caption: one line of the fault-find is wrong — find it
activities.name: esFaultSpot

config.prompt: A apprentice reasons through a dark lamp. One line is wrong — click it:
lines: Switch on, lamp dark — measure across the fitting
Full 230 V at the fitting: the supply is fine, so suspect the lamp itself (open-circuit)
Zero at the fitting but full voltage at the switch: the break lies between them
Current flows even through a broken path — that is what keeps a lamp lit
Scaled up — more switches, bigger cables, three phases — the habit is the same: measure before believing
config.correction: Current flows only when the path is whole — voltage appears where the circuit is complete and across the break.
config.why: Ohm's law read backwards: an open circuit carries no current, yet the full supply voltage appears across the open point — voltage tells you where the break is.
